Irrigation water quality impacts greatly on the specific design and maintenance requirements for recycled water irrigation systems. The type of treatment received by the reclaimed water prior to release or use determines specific water quality issues, so users of reclaimed water should know the treatment level of the source water. Level 1 treated reclaimed water may contain a variety of pathogens and solids and should never be applied by drinking water lines (U.S. EPA, 2004; Lazarova et al., 2004b).
Type of irrigation system
Sprinkler irrigation applies reclaimed water to the plants and can leave deposits of solids or solids containing salts on leaves and fruits. Deposits of salts may coat the root zone, resulting in salinity and water availability problems. Spray systems with high pressure and small nozzles are more susceptible to clogging with solids than other systems. Spray irrigation may also result in drift. Any fine mist created by sprinkler systems will be carried in the wind or air currents with a potential for drifting off the application area and onto unintended targets. The small particle size of mist allows for an increased surface area for salt crystals to accumulate which can be damaging to plants and soil.
A drip irrigation system applies reclaimed water directly to the plant’s root

Financial instruments are cash, a contractual right to receive or deliver cash, or evidence of an ownership interest in an entity.
Cash consists of notes and coins (and, in some jurisdictions, checks on demand at banks), and balances with central banks.
Financial instruments that give rise to a contractual right to receive or deliver cash are called financial assets.
Financial instruments that give rise to a contractual right to deliver or receive other financial instruments are called derivative financial instruments.
Financial instruments that give rise to an ownership interest in an entity are called equity instruments.
